rationale: Original Chinese application CN101664541A uses 川芎 (Chuanxiong) at 8–20 weight parts in a nine-herb oral dysmenorrhea formula. The claim-specific examples report mice/rats, not human trial data. Chinese Pharmacopoeia/USP identify Chuanxiong or Sichuan Lovage Rhizome as Ligusticum chuanxiong dried rhizome; this is not Levisticum officinale leaf. Pain and traditional use are adjacent context only; not a direct lovage-leaf/PD pain result. Source: https://patents.google.com/patent/CN101664541A/zh and grant https://patents.google.com/patent/CN101664541B/zh.

Original Chinese application CN101856398A uses 川芎 (Chuanxiong) at 22.4–44.8 weight parts with peony bark and borneol for a claimed chest/heart-pain remedy. Grant text reports pharmacology in mice (and other animal preparations), not an identified human clinical dataset; the general “clinical practice” assertion supplies no study design or participant results. USP defines Chuanxiong/Sichuan Lovage Rhizome as Ligusticum chuanxiong dried rhizome, distinct from accepted Kew taxon Levisticum officinale and its leaf. Related analgesia context, not Levisticum leaf or Parkinson pain evidence. Sources: https://patents.google.com/patent/CN101856398A/zh and https://patents.google.com/patent/CN101856398B/en.

Qishe Pill trial protocol includes Szechuan lovage rhizome in a multi-herb formula and specifies neck-pain severity in cervical radiculopathy. It is not Levisticum officinale leaf, is not Parkinson disease, and provides protocol rather than results; related botanical-name and pain context only. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24099350/

Agricultural-index appearance duplicates the MED record at rank 2 (PMID 40617359). Abstract reports isolated eugenol in paraquat-exposed Wistar rats with motor/cognitive measures, not whole culinary clove or human Parkinson executive function. Count as one study, not independent replication.

Eugenol, a major clove constituent, was administered to paraquat-exposed rats; cognition/memory and motor behavior were assessed. Isolated constituent, toxin model, and nonhuman outcomes are indirect, not ground clove spice treatment in Parkinson disease. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40617359/

Randomized 16-week olfactory training in type 2 diabetes with MCI used clove among six odorants and reported cognitive improvement including executive-function domains. Odor-only exposure in a mixed training regimen does not establish ground clove ingestion or clove-specific effects; no Parkinson cohort. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40908892/

Clove odor served as a control carrier in human experiments of androstadienone; it was not the assigned causal exposure. The abstract reports no effect on cognitive Stroop or general working memory attributable to clove, and no Parkinson or culinary clove intervention. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19470369/

Physics study observes motion of fruit, including blueberries, on a hotplate. No human or Parkinson participants, blueberry treatment, or voice/speech endpoint; “sound pressure level” occurs in a popcorn comparison and is a lexical collision. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34996974/

Forest musk deer olfactory-genome study notes receptor sequence potential for spearmint odor recognition. This is animal genomic context, not spearmint exposure or human olfactory-impairment treatment; no Parkinson sample or measured clinical smell outcome. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31106883/

Rats received soybean oil as a dietary control after hydrogenated vegetable-fat supplementation, then amphetamine/physical-activity protocols assessed addiction-related behavior and anxiety. Oil exposure is a comparator, not a daytime-sleepiness intervention; nonhuman and endpoint mismatch. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28964775/

Human anesthesia trial compares propofol emulsions containing different lipid amounts; the standard product contains soybean oil. Outcomes concern procedural sedation, recovery and injection pain, not daytime sleepiness, and soybean oil is an intravenous excipient rather than culinary intake. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15114202/
